      I, the Chairperson of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its
behalf, do hereby present this Hundred and Seventieth Report of the Committee.
.
1.2       The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on  29th August, 2007.
 
1.3       The notifications containing Rules/Regulations, etc. which were laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha during its 210 th Session
(February- March, April-May, 2007) have been perused by the Committee in the light of the provisions of the Acts under which these
were framed and also with a view to see whether these have been laid properly and within the prescribed time-frame.   The Committee’s
observations/recommendations are contained in the report that follows.
 
NEW DELHI
29th August, 2007
 
 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA
Chairperson
Committee on Subordinate Legislation,
Rajya Sabha
                                                            
 
 
Report
I

            During the 210
th  Session of the Rajya Sabha,     (23rd February to 21st March, 23rd April to 17th May,  2007) 186 Statutory Orders
relating to Rules/Regulations/Schemes/Bye-laws framed under the Constitution/ Acts of Parliament were laid on the Table of the House
by various Ministries/Departments. The details of the Gazette Notifications in which these were published, the date of their laying on the
Table of the Rajya Sabha have been indicated in the Ministry-wise statement placed at Annexure. Out of the above notifications that were
laid, there has been delay in laying of some of the notifications as per the details given below: -

2.         During the course of scrutiny of these Orders, the Committee has noted some cases where there has been a considerable time lag
between the date of notification of the Order and the date of its laying. The annexed statement also indicates the period of delay in cases
where notifications have not been laid as per the schedule prescribed by the Committee and where such notifications were accompanied
by a statement indicating the reasons for the delay in laying. In some of the cases the delay has been quite long. The
observations/recommendations of the Committee in respect of the specific Ministries/Departments are as follows: -  
           
(i) Ministry of Civil Aviation
 
            The Committee notes with regret that there has been a delay of up to eleven months on the part of the Ministry of Civil Aviation in
laying three of their notifications (Sl. Nos 2,3,& 4) and  in all the cases the Ministry have not appended the delay statements .
           
            The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation would avoid delay in laying of the notifications and in case of any delay
actually taking place in laying , a delay statement is invariably appended.
 
 
(ii) Ministry of Commerce & Industry (Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion)
 
           
 
      The Committee notes with regret that the Ministry of Commerce & Industry (Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion) have
delayed by three months the laying of their notification (Sl. No. 6).  The Ministry have not appended any delay statement even with the
said notification. The Committee hopes that the Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion shall take necessary steps to ensure that

        “Orders required to be laid before the House should be laid (i) if the House is not in Session, during the Session immediately
following the date of publication of the Order in the Official Gazette and (ii) if the House is in Session, on the date of the publication of
the Order, during its continuance and in case the time lag between the date of publication and the date of the closing of the Session is less
than 15 clear days, before the expiry of the Session immediately following the said Session. All the Ministries/Departments of
Government of India should henceforth comply with this schedule in the matter of laying of the Orders issued under various Acts of
Parliament on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.” (131

2.       During the course of scrutiny of these Orders, the Committee has noted some cases where there has been a
considerable time lag between the date of notification of the Order and the date of its laying. The annexed
statement also indicates the period of delay in cases where notifications have not been laid as per the schedule

file:///10.21.218.119/who%20am%20i/1%20rajesh%20sir/convert/english/Committee%20on%20Subordinate%20Legislation/171%20Report.htm[25-10-2016 16:42:29]
prescribed by the Committee and whether such notifications were accompanied by a statement indicating the
reasons for the delay in laying. In some of the cases the delay has been quite long. The
observations/recommendations of the Committee in respect of the specific Ministries/Departments are as follows:
-  
         
(i)        Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries 
 
          The Committee notes with regret that there has been a delay of 11 months and 9 months, respectively, in
laying of two notifications (Sl Nos. 1 & 2) and no delay statement was sent therewith.
 
          The Committee would like the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries to take corrective measures so as to
obviate such delay in future and in case such delays occur the notification while being laid before Parliament
should be accompanied  by statutes giving reason for the delay in laying.
    
(ii)     Ministry of Commerce & Industry (Department of Commerce)
 
          The Committee notes with regret that the Ministry of Commerce & Industry (Department of Commerce)
have delayed the laying of their notification (Sl. No. 4) by 3 months. The delay statement appended by the said
notification reads:-
 
          “The Coffee Board (Cadre & Recruitment) Rules, 1993 were framed by the Coffee Board in accordance with
the powers conferred by Rule 31 of the Coffee Board Rules, 1955.  As there was no provision under Rule 31 of the
Coffee Rules, 1955 regarding laying of the rules made thereunder, on the table of the Parliament, the same could
not be laid on the Table of each House of Parliament.
 
          However, the Rajya Sabha Committee on Subordinate Legislation were of the view that as per sub-section
(xv) of Section 48 of the Coffee Act, 1942, the rule making powers, in respect of Pay & allowances, leave and
other conditions of the service of the staff employed by the Board (other than those appointed by Central Govt.)
and other employees of the Board, are vested with the Central Govt. and as
such these rules should have been framed by the Central Govt. not by the Coffee Board.”
           The Committee regrets to note that the delay statement gives only the circumstance under which the
required rules have framed/laid but there is nothing in it to explain how the laying of the notification has been
delayed by three months.  The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Commerce & Industry (Department of
Commerce) would take note of discrepancy and avoid recurrence of the same in future.
 
 
(iii)              Ministry of Communications & Information Technology (Department of Information
Technology)
 
          The Committee notes with regret that there has been a delay of 10 months in laying of one notification (
Sl.No.7) and no delay statement was sent therewith.
         
          The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Communications & Information Technology (Department
of Information Technology) should strictly adhere to the time schedule as recommended by it and in case there is a
delay in laying the notification should invariably be accompanied by a delay statement explaining the reasons for
such delay.
 
(iv)              Ministry of Consumer affairs Food & Public Distribution (Department of Consumer Affairs)

          The Committee is unhappy to note that the two notifications (Sl.Nos.16 &17)  laid by the Ministry of
Consumer Affairs Food & Public Distribution (Department of Consumer Affairs) has been delayed by ( 1 Year Sl.
No. 16) and ( 10 months   Sl. No.17).  The Ministry have not appended any delay statement with the said
notifications.
          The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Consumer Affairs Food & Public Distribution (Department
of Consumer Affairs) should take necessary remedial steps to ensure that the statutory notifications are laid timely
as per the prescribed schedule.   Further, there has been considerable delay in laying these two notifications.   But
the Parliament has not been apprised of the reasons for such a long delay due to absence of the delay statement.  
The Committee hopes that such instances shall not recur
 
(v)     Ministry of Environment & Forests
 
          The Committee notes with regret the Ministry of Environment & Forests have delayed in laying one of their
notification by 11 months ( Sl. No. 26).  The Ministry have not appended delay statement with this notification.
 
The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Environment & Forests would avoid such instances of delay in the
laying of Subordinate Legislation in
future and, shall in such unavoidable circumstances keep the House informed of the reasons for delay in laying by
appending  a delay  statement.
 
(vi)              Ministry of External Affairs
          The Committee regrets to note that there is a delay of 8 months in laying of one out of the three notifications
laid by the Ministry of External Affairs (Sl. No. 29).  The Ministry have not appended a delay statement with the
delayed notification either.
 
         
 
 
The Committee hopes that the Ministry of External Affairs would avoid such delays and would append a delay
statement in all such cases of delay in future.
 
(vii)             Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (Department of Health)
 
          The Committee notes with regret that the lone notification (Sl. No.54) laid by the Ministry of Health &
Family Welfare (Department of Health) during the 211
th Session  has been delayed by  7 months and no delay
statement has been appended, even.
 
          The Committee hopes that the Ministry would take necessary corrective steps in the matter to avoid delay
and also invariably apprise Parliament of the causes of delay at the time of laying by appending a delay statement.  
 
(viii)  The Ministry of Home Affairs
 
          The Committee is unhappy to note that out of the 11 notifications laid by the Ministry of Home Affairs, there
has been delay upto 1 year and eleven months in the laying of three notifications (Sl. Nos. 62-64).  The Ministry
have not appended delay statement with any of these delayed notifications either.
 
          The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should stick to the time schedule as

recommended by it in its 131 st Report in the matter of laying of Subordinate Legislation before Parliament and in
case of any delay a  delay statement must also be appended so as to apprise the Parliament of the reasons that  have

(ix)              Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of Secondary and Higher Education)
 
     The Committee notes with serious concern that the Ministry of Human Resource Development have unusually
delayed the laying of their notification (Sl.No.66) abnormally by 1 year and one month.  The delay statement

          UGC (Minimum Qualifications required for the appointment and career advancement of teachers in
universities and institutions affiliated to it) (Second Amendment Regulations, 2006) was notified on 19 th August,
2006.  Required number of Gazette copies of the said Regulation (both in Hindi and English) has been received in

The Edible Oils Packaging (Regulation) Order, 1998.

and a questionnaire on the subject was forwarded to the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution,
(Directorate of Vanaspati, Vegetable Oils & Fats) on the 29
th September, 1999 for their comments/clarifications thereon.   The
Ministry vide their O.M. dated the 26 th May, 2000 furnished their comments/clarifications on each point raised in the
questionnaire. The points referred to the Ministry and their comments/clarifications thereon are reproduced below: -

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

1.       Point raised
Whether the Edible Oils Packaging (Regulation) Order, 1998 has been laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha, if so, the
details in this regard.
Ministry’s Comments
41 copies of the Edible Oils Packaging (Regulation) Order, 1998 issued vide Notification NO. GSR. 584 (E) dated 17-
09-1998 and Corrigendum No. GSR 702 (E) dated 30-11-1998 alongwith one copy of each in Hindi and in English
authenticated by the Minister (Consumer Affairs and Public Distribution) were sent to both Lok Sabha and Rajya  Sabha
Secretariats on 10-12-1998 vide this Directorate’s letter No. 17/1/98-EXP. dated 09-12-1998. While information from Lok
Sabha regarding laying of the papers on the Table on 15-12-1998 (vide Lok Sabha Bulletin Part –I No. 58) has been received,
the information from Rajya Sabha has not be received so far.
 
2.       Point raised- 
Clause 2(b)
          “Edible Oils” mean  vegetable oils and fats and include any i.e, margarine, vanaspati, bakery shorting and fat spread as
specified in the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (37 of 1954) and rules made there under, for human consumption;”
Whether the term “edible oils” include ghee and butter also and if not, the justification for non-inclusion of these items
within the meaning of the term.
Ministry’s Comments
The term “Edible Oils” does not include ghee and butter, as ghee and butter are of animal origin and not of vegetable
origin. The term “edible oils” means vegetable oil as per the definition of “edible oils”
 
3.       Point raised- Clause 2(c)
          “Edible Oils Commissioner” means the person appointed as Edible Oils Commissioner by the Central Government and
includes any other person empowered by the Central Government to exercise any or all of the functions of the Edible Oils
commissioner under this Order;”
Whether there are any qualifications or conditions precedent to empowering any person to exercise any or all the
functions of the Edible Oil Commissioner and if so, whether Government have any objection in prescribing them in the Order
itself.
Ministry’s Comments
No qualification has been explicitly stated. The implicit understanding is that the person empowered to exercise the
functions of the Edible Oils Commissioner would be a Senior Gazetted Officer of the Central/ State Government competent
enough to handle the responsibility of the job assigned and enjoying the confidence of the superiors.
 
Action Taken
Modified the provision of Clause 2 (c) of the Order vide notification dated 22 nd November, 2005 (Annexure VII-
Appendix ‘A’)
 
4.       Point raised- 
Clause 3(b)
          “which is not packed in a container, marked and labeled in the manner as specified in the Scheule-1:
                  Provided that the State Government may, in the public interest, for reasons to be recorded in writing, in specific
circumstances and for a specific period by a notification in the Official Gazette, exempt any edible oil from the provisions of
this Order.”
What is the justification for empowering the State Governments to exempt any edible oil from the provisions of this
Order? What are the specific circumstances in the mind of the Ministry behind prescribing for such exemption? Further, there

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///10.21.218.119/who%20am%20i/1%20rajesh%20sir/convert/english/Committee%20on%20Subordinate%20Legislation/172%20Report.htm[25-10-2016 16:42:19]
is no provision in the clause under which the State Government is under any obligation to inform the Central Government or
the Edible Oils Commissioner regarding the exemption given to any edible oil. Whether such information is not desirable in the
opinion of Government; what is the reaction of the Ministry in this regard? Whether these provisions are being implemented in
a foolproof manner?
Ministry’s Comments
The Central Government is aware of the fact that the production of edible oils is highly decentralized. Substantial
quantity is produced in the small scale or unorganized sector. Further, a sizeable portion of the population is living below the
poverty line. It is in view of these situations that the State Governments have been empowered to exempt any edible oil from
the provisions of this Order in specific circumstances and for specific period only in the public interest for reasons to be
recorded in writing and for specific period only.
          Further vide 
Clause 15, the Edible Oil Commissioner has been authorized to issue appropriate directions including
seeking of information from the State Governments for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of the Packaging Order.
 
5.       Point raised- Clause 4(1) read with Schedule-III
“Registration: No person shall carry on business as a packer except under a certificate of registration granted to him
under this Order and in accordance with the terms and conditions specified in the Schedule-III.”
One of the terms and conditions for grant of certificate of registration is that the registered packer shall not employ any
person who is suffering from infection/contagious disease which is likely to affect packing in hygienic conditions. Which is the
authority that would determine whether any particular disease is infectious or contagious; whether Government have any
objection in prescribing the competent authority in the Order itself? Further, it has been made obligatory for each registered
packer to maintain a register showing the quantity sold. Is it not possible that a registered packer may not be engaging himself
in selling, the product and that he might be doing only the packaging work, in that case such a registered packer would not be
able to comply with this condition and he would be unable to keep a record of the edible oil sold. Whether Government have
any objection in suitable modification of this condition? 
Ministry’s Comments
The power for implementation of the Packaging Order is delegated to the State Governments. It has been left to the State
Governments to decide as to how they will carry-out the various provisions of the order. We have already written to the State
Governments that in case there is any operational difficulty in the implementation of the Order, these may be brought to the
notice of the Central Government so as to resolve the issue in a manner which is not inconsistent with the provisions of this
Order.

Clause 4(2)
          “Every person who intends to carry on the business of a packer shall make an application to registering authority in the

by the State Government.”
The provision does not specify the quantum of fee to be paid to the State Government along with the application form to

Ministry’s Comments
          As already indicated, the power for implementation of the Packaging Order has been delegated to the State Government.
It has been left to the State Government to specify the quantum of fee having regard to the local situations etc.
 
7.       Point raised- Clause 4(3)
“No person shall be eligible for grant of certificate of registration under this Order unless he has his own laboratory

facilities and has appointed in that laboratory at least one chemist having Bachelor of Science Degree with Chemistry as one

Ministry’s Comments
Same as replied under Question No. 5.

As per the provisions, there has been a further delegation of powers upon the Edible Oils Commissioner with regard to

prescribing other conditions to be complied with by a registered packer. What is the justification for delegating such powers on

(1)     Point referred
          Whether the Bombay Port (Licensing and Control of Pilots) Regulations, 1975 have since been laid on the Table
of both the Houses and if, so the date of laying thereof.
Ministry’s reply
          When these regulations were framed in 1975, there was no provision in the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 for
placing of regulations before both Houses of Parliament.  This requirement was introduced by insertion of provision by
Act 17 of 1982 with effect from 31.5.1982.
Committee’s observation
          The Committee was appraised that the regulations were not laid on the table of both the Houses as there was no
laying provision in the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 prior to 1982.  The Committee desired that the regulations should
be laid now alongwith the amendments suggested by it.
(2)     Point referred: Regulation 1 (2)
          “They shall come into force on the date of the publication of the Government’s sanction in the Official Gazette.”
          Generally the rules/regulations are brought into effect from the date of publication of the Official Gazette. What
is the significance of publication of “Government’s sanction” in case of the rules in hand?
Ministry’s reply
          Section 124 (1) of the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 provides that no regulation made by the Board under the Act
(other than a regulation made under sub-section 2 of section 17) shall have effect until it has been approved by the
Central Government and until such approval has been published in the Official Gazette.   The provision in the
regulation is accordingly worded for the regulations to come into effect from date of publication of Government’s
sanction in the Gazette.   In effect, however, the regulations came into effect from the date of publication in the
Gazette.
Committee’s observation
          The management of the board had agreed to amend the commencement clause as suggested by the Committee.
(3)     Point referred: Regulation 3 - Definitions
          The term “pilot” is generally associated with the aeroplanes .  But here it has been used for handling of vessels. 
Whether Government have any objection in inserting the definition of word “Pilot” in the regulation itself?
Ministry’s reply
          The term ‘Pilot’ is defined in the Indian Ports Act, 1908, section 3 (3) as under:
          ‘Pilot’ means a person for the time being authorized by Government to pilot vessels.”
          It is a term in the standard international maritime vocabulary.  Hence, it is not included in the definition in the
regulations.
 
(4)     Point referred: Regulation 7-Conditions for joining the pilot service
          “A person shall not be licensed as a pilot unless and until he satisfies the Chairman that he fulfills the following
conditions, namely:-
(a)     The conditions of eligibility for direct recruitment to posts under the Board as may be laid down by
regulations in this behalf;
(b)     on the date of appointment as a probationary pilot he is of an age not below 25 years and not above 35
years, unless otherwise relaxed by the Chairman; and

(c)     he possesses the qualifications specified in regulation 8.”
(a)      The regulation mentions about the eligibility for direct recruitment.   Whether there is any quota for the
departmental candidates for joining the pilot service?
(b)     Whether any specific regulations have been framed for direct recruitment in pilot service.   Whether such
regulations can be incorporated in these regulations itself?
(c)     Sub-regulation (c) appears to be superfluous in view of regulation 8.  Whether the Ministry have any
objection in deleting this sub-regulation?
Ministry’s reply
(a)      There is no quota prescribed for departmental candidates for appointment to the post of Pilot.  The reason
is that the qualifications required for the Pilot can be acquired only with service on foreign sea-going vessels and not in
the Port.
(b)     Yes, separate regulations covering appointment to all posts in the Port including that of Pilot have been
framed which are known as the Mumbai Port Trust Employees (Recruitment, Seniority and Promotion) Regulations,
1976.  The basic educational and other requirements are prescribed therein.   These are the same as prescribed in
regulation 8 (1) (a) in these regulations.
(c)     Clause (c) of regulation 7 interalia is one of the conditions for joining the Port’s pilotage service.  The said
clause provides that the candidates must fulfill the prescribed qualifications.  Regulation 8 specifies such qualifications
for joining Port’s pilotage service.
(5)     Point referred: Regulation 8 (1) (a) - Qualification of Candidates
“A candidate for a pilotage license shall:
(a) produce certificate of good character and sobriety and be in possession of a Certificate of Competency as
Master (Foreign-going) granted by the Government of India or its equivalent and should have, preferably experience
of at least six months as First Mate on a foreign-going ship.”
The words ‘its equivalent’ are vague.  Whether Government have any objection in making the provision of
Regulation 8 (1) (a) specific?
Ministry’s reply
As per Section 86 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, the Central Government may, by notification in the
Official Gazette, declare any certificate of competency granted under the laws in force in any other country as
equivalent to the corresponding certificate of competency or service granted under this Act.  This is to facilitate Indian
nationals obtaining equivalent competency certificates in other countries to seek employment opportunities in India
and on Indian ships.  The countries so recognized may change from time to time.   Hence, the inclusion of the words
‘its equivalent’ in the regulation.
(6)     Point referred: Regulation 8 (2)
          “The fee for a pilot’s licence and for renewal thereof in case of loss shall be prescribed by the Board from time
to time.”
What is the existing rate of pilot fee prescribed by the Board, when this fee was last revised?
Ministry’s reply
The fee prescribed for issue or renewal of pilot’s licence is Rs.30.  This was fixed in July 1975.
Committee’s observation
The Committee desired that the fee for a pilot’s licence should be revised suitably and in case no fee is charged
from the pilots for a licence, the provision is irrelevant and it should be scrapped.
(7)     Point referred: Regulation 10 - Examination Committee
          “The examination shall be conducted by the Examination Committee composed as follows:
(i)               The Deputy Conservator (Chairman)

(ii)             The Harbour Master

What is the manner in which the examination is conducted, whether it is written or practical or both.  The
regulation seems to be silent on these aspects, are there separate set of rules/regulations for this?
Ministry’s reply
          The candidate is required to undergo practical training for a period of about 5 months during which time he
attends vessel being piloted by senior pilots and where he gets an opportunity to observe maneuvres  both during day
and night.  The Examination Committee takes into account the regularity and attendance of the candidate on the ships
and his performance with regard to the various aspects of ship’s manoeuvres  in different parts of harbour and the
docks, his interests and capabilities in understanding the technical aspects of navigation as also his ability to pilot a
ship considering the tidal, wind and weather conditions.   The Examination Committee consisting of the 5 persons
including an expert from outside conducts oral examination on all the above-mentioned aspects as well as the subjects
mentioned under regulation 9.  There are no separate set of rules/regulations for conduct of the examination.
(8)     Point referred: Regulation 11 - Failure to pass an examination
          “In the event of a probationary pilot failing to pass the specified examination within nine months of his
appointment, he will be liable to be discharged.”
          How many trials a probationer gets during the period of 9 months.?  To what extent, the provision of this
regulation has been invoked  in the past i.e. service of probationers terminated, are any options available to the
probationers after the invoking of Regulation 11, if so the details?
 
Ministry’s reply
          The period of nine months for passing the examination indicated in the copy of the regulations submitted earlier
is incorrect.  The mistake is regretted.   In fact, this period has since been revised to twelve months.  The prescribed
training period is six months.  Thereafter, the candidate can appear for the examination upto another six months. 
There is no limit on the number of attempts to appear for the examination during this period.
          Occasions of termination of service of probationers on failure to pass the examination are rare.  During the last
10 years, there has been no such incident.
          Though the persons are recruited as Probationary Pilot, their actual working starts after completion of training,
passing of the examination and issue of licence.   Thus, the examination is a part of the recruitment process.  Strict
training is given to the candidates followed by ample opportunity to clear the examination.   If the person still does not
clear the examination, he is not suitable for the post.  It is, therefore, not necessary to provide for any option for appeal
or review.
 (9)    Point referred: Regulation 25 - Master Pilots to give instructions to Junior Pilots and Probationary
Pilots
          “The Master Pilots shall assist in instructing the junior pilots and probationary pilots in all branches of a pilot’s
duty.
What is the meaning of the words “assist in instructing” ?; should it not be substituted by the words “assist and
instruct” so as to be more clear and specific?
Ministry’s reply
          Yes; ‘assist and instruct’ would be the more appropriate phrase.  Suitable change will be made in the regulations.

(10)    Point referred: Regulation 27 - Pilots to obey the orders of the authority
          “A Pilot shall obey and execute all orders and regulations given or issued by the Board, the Chairman, the

He shall also obey all orders given by the Dock Masters relating to the docking, undocking, towing, transportation or

Regulation 28-Pilot’s behaviour
“A pilot shall at all times exercise strict sobriety.  He shall, throughout the time he is in charge of vessel, use his
utmost care and diligence for her safety and the safety of other vessels and property.  He shall when necessary keep
the lead going while the vessel is underway.  He shall not lay by the vessel aground without a written order from the
owner or officer in command.”
(a)      Whether the Board has prescribed any code of conduct for the pilots, and if so, whether the same cannot
be made part of the regulations?
(b)     What action is taken for violation of code of conduct?
Ministry’s reply
(a)      The Board has not prescribed any code of conduct specifically for the Pilots apart from the above
provisions of regulations 27 and 28.  However, Mumbai Port Trust Employees (Conduct) Regulations, 1976, which
contain various regulations regarding discipline, integrity, devotion to duty, etc., are applicable to all employees of the
Port including the Pilots.  Since the Pilots perform certain specific tasks relating to navigation, docking, undocking,
towing, mooring, etc. of the ships, in addition, certain specific provisions have been made in these regulations, namely,
in regulations 27 and 28.
(b)     Violation of code of conduct under regulations 27 and 28 and the general code of conduct prescribed
under the Mumbai Port Trust Employees (Conduct) Regulations, 1976 invites action/penalty under the Mumbai Port
Trust Employees (Classification, Control & Appeal) Regulations, 1976.
(11)    Point referred: Regulation 33 - Pilot may leave vessel at anchor in the 
harbour if not provided with
proper food and sleeping accommodation
          “The Master of a vessel in pilotage  charge of a Pilot shall provide the Pilot with reasonable accommodation, if
necessary, and with breakfast between 7.00 a.m., with lunch between 8.00 p.m., if the vessel is at anchor in the
harbour during these hours.  In the event of failure on the part of the Master of the vessel, the pilot may leave the
vessel and come to shore after giving the officer in command at least one hour’s notice in writing of his intention to do
so and shall report the case in writing to the Deputy Conservator as soon as practicable.”
(a)      What is implied by the term – “reasonable accommodation”?
(b)     To what extent the provisions of regulation 33 are still being implemented, are these provisions which
require reporting in writing twice not obsolete in the present day scenario?
Ministry’s reply
(a)      Reasonable accommodation means an accommodation which would provide the pilot adequate comfort
and be suitable to his status under the attendant circumstances and conditions.  Usually, as a matter of international
practice, all sea-going vessels have specified accommodation for pilot known as Pilot’s cabin.
(b)     The provision is not so relevant in today’s scenario where berthing of vessel does not take such long time
as before nor does a vessel needs to stay for long period at anchorage awaiting docking.  However, if the rare occasion
of a pilot having to leave the vessel does arise, giving of notice to Master of the vessel is necessary.  Likewise, report
to the Dy. Conservator is essential to have full information and enable enquiry into the situation and taking of
corrective action as may be necessary.

1.       Point raised
Rule 5: Vacancies
“The Board may, in consultation with its Sponsor Bank, determine the number of vacancies in each category of
posts to be filled keeping in view, the guidelines issued by Central Government from time to time.”
(i)                What are the present Guidelines of the Central Government in this regard?

Ministry’s reply
The Central Government has issued the norms and guidelines for creation and filling of the vacancies in various
cadres and appointments and promotion to the newly created posts from time to time.   Recently, the Government of
India has constituted a Working Group to review the staffing norm in RRBs.  The Working Group is likely to submit

Committee’s Observation
The Committee felt that RRBs should give some autonomy for recruitment of staff.  The Committee noted that
the recruitment was temporarily banned in order to re-adjust the surplus staff and that the surplus staff could be
redeployed from one bank to another.   The Committee further noted that RRBs could also hire people on contract

In terms of Government of India letter No.7 (5)/2004-RRB dated 2.11.2004, (Annexure-I)  freedom has been

(5)/2004-RRB dated 4.8.2005 (Annexure-II) .  Accordingly, the sponsor banks are required to re-assess the manpower

What are the other agencies to which reference is made for filling up of vacancies?   In what manner the

Ministry’s reply
The reserved vacancies in the Group ‘C’ are required to be filled up in the RRBs as per the procedure indicated
in Chapter 7 of the Brochure on reservation for SC/ST – (8th edition) which are as under:
i)                   All the vacancies should be notified to the local/regional Employment Exchange.
ii)                 When a local Employment Exchange is unable to nominate any suitable candidate, it will refer vacancies to the
Central Employment Exchange.
iii)
               If sufficient numbers of SC/ST candidates are not available through Employment Exchange the vacancies
should be advertised in local newspapers.
iv)
               Simultaneously, with the advertisement, the vacancies should be brought to the notice of the SC/ST
organisations listed in Appendix 11 to be said Brochure.  While doing so, it should be made clear to such organisations
that their function is limited to advising the SC/ST candidates about the recruitment proposed and that it will not be for
them to recommend or press the names of any individuals.   The candidates should apply to the appointing authority
either direct or through the Employment Exchange as the case may be.
As against the above instructions, Rule 10 indicates that the reference is required to be made out to the Other
Agencies also in addition to the Employment Exchange and the Jila Sainik Board.  Further, the second proviso to the
said rule also states that no candidate other than those sponsored by the Employment Exchange, Sainik Board or Other

informed, when the required numbers of candidates are not available through Employment Exchange/Sainik Board and
these agencies do not have powers to sponsor the name of the candidates.  In view of the above, Rule 10 is slightly at
variance with the above guidelines in the Brochure.  Accordingly, the Government will consider amending Rule 10 in
consultation with the Ministry of Law.

The Committee desired that the procedure as laid down in Rule 10(1) needs to be realigned so as to resolve the

4.       Point raised
Schedule-III
Against the eligibility column for various posts covered in the schedule, a minimum period of service has been
prescribed which the officer should have rendered before he is eligible to be considered for promotion to the next
higher scale.  In the same breath, there is a proviso for relaxation in the qualifying service for a period up to 2 years,
in case eligible officers are not available.
Normally, the Rule lays down the eligibility criteria only and in case any relaxation is called for, the powers are
exercised under a general clause in the Rule providing the Competent Authority with the powers to relax in certain
cases.  The pattern followed in the Third Schedule i.e. providing for relaxation in the qualifying service in case of each
of the post separately is a deviation from the normal procedure more particularly because the power to relax in the
Rules is exercisable only in extreme cases of hardship and for removal of disability, is any.  On the other hand, in the
present case, the power to relax the condition of length of service has been made to form a part of the eligibility
criteria thereby giving an impression that the eligibility condition can be relaxed in a routine manner in case eligible
persons are not available.
What is the justification for adopting a changed pattern in the rules in hand and whether Government have any
objection in recasting the provisions in the changed pattern?
Ministry’s reply
The Rule specifically lays down a criterion, which stipulates that relaxation is to be made only if eligible officers
are not available.  This relaxation can be made only with the prior approval of the National Bank who will ensure that
this is not done in a routine manner.
Committee’s Observation
The Committee noted the clarification given by the Ministry during the course of discussions that relaxations are
not made in a routine manner.  The Committee, however, felt that the circumstances for allowing relaxation should
really deserve and that it should be on a case-to-case basis and that the reasons for the same should be required to be
recorded.  The Ministry agreed to the Committee’s suggestions.
Action taken
While allowing relaxations, NABARD ensures on a case by case basis that there are no other eligible officers
available and that all the criteria prescribed for allowing relaxation are satisfied.

when any official from these categories is to be considered by the Committee. Whether Government have any
objection in substituting the word “may” by the word “shall”?
Ministry’s reply
The word “may” used in the relevant rule has the connotation of “shall”.   The Committee constituted under this
rule invariably comprises of members belonging to SC/STs.

6.       Point raised
Schedule-III
For appointment to the posts in the Schedule, the method of promotion has been stated to be on the basis of
seniority-cum-merit.
What are the main features of this procedure for promotion; Whether it is permissible to change the seniority of
officials as it exists in the feeder grade while recommending their names for promotion to the next higher grade which
is inherent in the “selection” as a method of promotion at least for the purpose of promotion in scale III, scale II and
scale I so as to promote merit in the organisation?
Ministry’s reply
“Seniority-cum-merit” shall mean seniority and found fit for promotion.   It is not possible to change the
seniority of officials, as it exists in the feeder grade.  Thus, seniority-cum-merit implies promotions based on seniority
subject to minimum necessary merit requisite for the promotion.  The Government feels that there should be a uniform
criterion for promotion to all scales and that the present system may continue.
Committee’s Observation
The Committee came across divergent views on the point of promotion on the basis of seniority-cum-merit.  The
Bank of Rajasthan was of the view that promotion should not be purely on the basis of seniority only and merit should
also be given at least 50% weight age.  The Dungarpur Banswara Gramin Bank was of the view that in lower scales,
weight age may be given to seniority but in higher scale merit should prevail.   The Gramin Bank was of the view that
promotion should be made on the basis of both seniority and merit.  The Committee reiterated the need for balance
between seniority and merit to keep the Regional Rural Banks competitive with the other commercial banks.
Action taken
The existing recruitment rules provide for filling up the posts by seniority-cum-merit.   It, therefore, gives due
weightage to the seniority as well as merit.    However, the position would be reviewed after the process for
amalgamation is completed.

Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules-2002
 
          The Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 framed under the Securitisation  & Reconstruction of
Financial Assets & Enforcement of Security Interest Ordinance, 2002 were examined and a questionnaire was
forwarded to the Ministry of Finance (Banking Division) on the 24th November, 2003, to which the Ministry replied
on the 7th May, 2004. The Committee considered the Ministry’s reply at its meeting held on 17 th November, 2005
and decided to seek further clarification on point No.1 (Rule 2 (d) defining ‘Approved Valuer’). The Ministry vide
their communication dated 29 th November, 2006 provided the requisite clarification and also gave details of the
changes carried out by the Ministry on the other points on Committee’s suggestion.

reproduced below: -
 
1.       Point raised- Rule 2(d) -
“Approved valuer” means a valuer  as approved by the Board of Directors or Board of Trustees of the
secured creditor, as the case may be.
Should the approved valuer  not be duly qualified; what is the justification for giving full discretion to the
secured creditor in this regard?
 
          Ministry’s 
comments : (7.5. 2004)
Approved valuer means the professional who is qualified to value the property for a fee.  It is difficult to
work out clear-cut definition making exhaustive list of approved valuers  in different fields and types of properties
that are to be valued.   It is, however, suggested that banks and financial institutions may be advised to utilize the
services of valuers through Institution of Valuers  who claimed to be the only registered body in the country and
their members are bound by code of conduct prescribed by it.  They are covered by fee prescribed by the
Government under Rule 8C of the Wealth Tax Act and also by CBDT.
 
 
Action Taken by the 
Ministry : (29.11.2006)
In terms of Rule 8(5) of Security Enforcement Rules, 2002, before effecting sale of immovable property, the
authorized officer is required to obtain valuation of the property from an approved valuer and in consultation with
the secured creditor, fix the reserve price of the property.  Chapter VII-B (Section 34 AB) of Wealth Tax Act, 1957

provides for registration of valuers.  Any person who possesses the qualifications prescribed under Rule 8A of
Wealth Tax Rules, 1957, may apply to the Chief Commissioner or Director General for being registered as a valuer
under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.  In terms of Rule 8A ibid, different qualifications have been prescribed for valuers

AB of Wealth Tax Act, 1957 and approved by the Board of Directors or Board of Trustees of the secured creditor,
as the case may be”.

Where the possession of the secured assets to be taken by the secured creditor are movable property in
possession of the borrower, the authorized officer shall take possession of such movable property in the presence of

rules
Are these two witnesses, the witnesses, of the secured creditor or they are the public/independent witnesses;
should the rule not clarify on this point?
 
          Ministry’s 
comments : (7.5. 2004)
Witnesses could be any one.  Flexibility in this matter is desirable and is recognized by the legislation as well
as judiciary.   No clarification in the Rule is necessary, as the present provision does not confine witnesses to
specific classes of persons.
 
3.       Point raised- Rule 4(3)
The authorized officer shall keep the property taken possession under sub-rules (1) either in his own custody
or in the custody of any person authorized or appointed by him, who shall take as much care of the property in his
custody as an owner of ordinary prudence would, under the similar circumstances, take of such property.
                            
 
This rule involves further delegation of power by the authorized officer to any person authorized or appointed
by him without fixing any responsibility either to the authorized officer or the person so authorized or appointed by
him in case there is any damage to the movable property in custody inadvertently.   Should the rule not vest ultimate
responsibility on the authorised officer even in case where he has authorized some body in this behalf?
 
Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
In terms of Rule 4(3), the Authorised  Officer shall take as much care of the property in his custody as owner
of ordinary prudence.  Further as per Rule 4(4), the Authorised Officer shall take steps for preservation and
protection of secured assets and insure them, if necessary, till they are sold or otherwise disposed of.  Therefore
even though the Authorised Officer is empowered to entrust the possession to others; he is still responsible for acts
of the custodian appointed by him to keep the assets.  Moreover, in terms of Section 19 of the Act, if the DRT or
DRAT holds the possession of secured assets by the secured creditor as wrongful and directs the secured creditor to

return such assets to the borrower, such borrower shall be entitled to payment of such compensation and costs as

4.       Point raised- Rule 5
Valuation of movable secured assets: After taking possession under sub-rule (1) of the Rule 4 and
in any case before sale, the authorized officer shall obtain the estimated value of the movable secured
assets and thereafter, if considered necessary, fix in consultation with the secured creditor, the reserve

          Ministry’s

In the light of the Supreme Court observations in Haryana Financial Corporation V.Jagadamba  (2002) 110
Comp. Case 20 (SC), notice of intended sale to the defaulting borrower is sufficient and any procedure requiring the
defaulting borrower to be associated or consulted in every stage in the sale of secured assets will place unnecessary

Authorised Officer is expected to secure the maximum sale price of the property to be sold.

          We propose to amend the title to the Pension Regulations, 2002 suitably by a Notification, which

copy of the amendment would be forwarded in due course.
 
          Committee’s further Observations (22.02.05):-
 
          The Ministry have stated that the Small Industries Development Bank of India Pension Regulations,
1993 were not notified. The Committee desired to know the justification for not notifying the said
regulations.
 
          Ministry’s further Comments (13.06.05):-
 
          SIDBI was created out of IDBI w.e.f. April 02, 1990 as per SIDBI Act, 1989. Since its formation,
SIDBI is following the service regulations and all other rules relating to the service matters as that of IDBI.
IDBI Pension Regulations were notified in 1995 and have been made applicable w.e.f. November 01, 1993.
In terms of the sixth bi-partie settlement between the IBA and the unions/associations of the bank
employees, the pension scheme was introduced in the nationalized banks w.e.f. November 01, 1993, but
notified in 1995. SIDBI also formulated the Pension Regulations in 1993 in anticipation of approval of the
Government. During the course of the consideration of the pension regulations, the question of constituting
Pension Fund had arisen and it was considered that since SIDBI had been granted tax exemption, there may
not be any need of constituting a separate Pension Fund. On further consideration of the matter, it was felt
to explore the possibility of adopting the pattern of RBI & NABARD Employee Gratuity and
Superannuation Fund Regulations instead of having a separate Pension Regulations in line with IDBI,
which had become a tax paying corporate entity. It, therefore, necessitated an exercise afresh to draft the
SIDBI Employee Gratuity and Superannuation Fund Regulations in line with RBI Regulations. Due to the
above development and subsequent developments like divestment of shares of IDBI in SIDBI and other
allied developments, the Pension Regulations of SIDBI were revisited and SIDBI Pension Regulations,
2002 were notified. It may be pertinent to mention that due to the late notification of the SIDBI Pension
Regulations, the employees have not been affected in any manner as the said Pension Regulations cover
employees from the date of creation of SIDBI subject to fulfillment of conditions.
